renderings.Rackham: If therefore among the ends at which our actions aim there be one which we will for its own sake, while we will the others only for the sake of this, and if we do not choose everything for the sake of something else (which would obviously result in a process ad infinitum, so that all desire would be futile and vain), it is clear that this one ultimate End must be the Good, and indeed the Supreme Good.
renderings.Ross: If, then, there is some end of the things we do, which we desire for its own sake (everything else being desired for the sake of this), and if we do not choose everything for the sake of something else (for at that rate the process would go on to infinity, so that our desire would be empty and vain), clearly this must be the good and the chief good.
renderings.Ostwald: Now, if there exists an end in the realm of action which we desire for its own sake, an end which determines all our other desires; if, in other words, we do not make all our choices for the sake of something else—for in this way the process will go on infinitely so that our desire would be futile and pointless—then obviously this end will be the good, that is, the highest good.
renderings.Peters: If then in what we do there be some end which we wish for on its own account, choosing all the others as means to this, but not every end without exception as a means to something else (for so we should go on ad infinitum, and desire would be left void and objectless)⁠—this evidently will be the good or the best of all things.

patterns.summary: Neuter adjectives, articles, and pronouns get a noun the Greek does not have: 'Good', 'end', 'science', 'thing', 'achievement'.
patterns.translators: Rackham most (e.g. 'this one ultimate End', 'this Supreme Good'); Ross least, who often keeps 'it' or 'that'.

patterns.summary: Words left understood in Greek are carried over from an earlier clause: the verb of wanting in sentence 1, the modal in sentence 6, 'to get' in sentence 10.
patterns.translators: All four do it; Ross and Ostwald also repeat verbs the Greek gives only once ('they should learn them', 'each must attain').

patterns.summary: Impersonal forms become personal ('we must try' for πειρατέον), genitives of belonging get a verb ('belongs to', 'is the object of'), and participles become 'since', 'that', or relative clauses.
patterns.translators: All four; Peters goes furthest, turning a question into a statement and 'it is welcome' into 'glad as one would be'.

patterns.summary: The potential optative with ἄν is usually 'must be', and φαίνεται with a predicate is either 'seems' or 'is clearly'.
patterns.translators: Rackham and Ross use 'must' most; Ostwald gives 'will be', 'is', or 'seems to'; Rackham and Ostwald read φαίνεται as 'clearly is'.

patterns.summary: Small particles (δέ, γε, γάρ, ποτε, and καί meaning 'even' or 'also') often have no English at all.
patterns.translators: Rackham renders the most ('while', 'also', 'exactly', 'Now'); Ostwald and Peters the fewest.

patterns.summary: Key terms shift between versions: δύναμις is 'faculty', 'capacity', or 'art'; ἐπιστήμη 'science' or 'branch of knowledge'; ἀρχιτεκτονική 'master-craft', 'master art', or 'master science'.
patterns.translators: Each translator is consistent with himself; Peters departs most from the others, and Ross and Rackham agree most.

patterns.summary: English sentence breaks do not match the Greek: Rackham and Ostwald split sentence 8 in two, while Ross joins 5 to 8 and 9 to 10, Rackham 5 to 7, Ostwald 4 to 5, and Peters 9 to 10.
patterns.translators: Ross joins the most; Ostwald splits and joins about equally; Peters keeps closest to the Greek breaks.
